questions.question: From the alternatives given below, choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'talk a blue streak'.

options.text: To speak with great rapidity, volume, and/or intensity
To use profane language with great rapidity and intensity
Enjoying a series of concurrent fortunate outcomes or occurrences
To have a series of concurrent fortunate outcomes or occurrences

questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'Option (1)' i.e. **To speak with great rapidity, volume, and/or intensity**.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The idiom **'talk a blue streak'** means to speak very rapidly and without stopping for a long time. (बहुत तेज़ी से और लगातार बोलना)
 
 
• **Example: **My aunt can **talk a blue streak** when she starts discussing her garden and all the plants she is growing.
 
 
 
• The phrase **'to speak with great rapidity, volume, and/or intensity'** correctly captures the essence of the idiom, which emphasizes the speed and continuous nature of the speech. (बहुत तेज़ी, ज़ोर और/या तीव्रता के साथ बोलना)
 
 
• **Example: **The witness began to **talk a blue streak** as soon as the lawyer finished asking the question.
 
 
 
• Hence, we can conclude that the meaning of the given idiom is to speak very quickly and with high energy.

Therefore, the correct answer is- **To speak with great rapidity, volume, and/or intensity**.

**Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

 
• **To use profane language **(अपशब्दों या अश्लील भाषा का प्रयोग करना): This refers to using words that are offensive or show a lack of respect for sacred things.
 
 
• **Example: **The player was removed from the game for using **profane language** against the referee.
 
 
 
• **Enjoying a series of concurrent fortunate outcomes **(लगातार सौभाग्यशाली परिणामों का आनंद लेना): This refers to experiencing a 'winning streak' or a period of continuous good luck.
 
 
• **Example: **After winning three matches in a row, the team is **enjoying a series of concurrent fortunate outcomes**.
 
 
 
• **To have a series of concurrent fortunate occurrences **(लगातार सौभाग्यशाली घटनाओं का होना): This is similar to a 'stroke of luck' or having a period where everything goes right.
 
 
• **Example: **It was a **series of concurrent fortunate occurrences** that led to him finding his lost wallet and winning the lottery on the same day.

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?

The chef is preparing a gourmet meal for the gala tonight.

options.text: A gourmet meal was being prepared by the chef for the gala tonight.
A gourmet meal is being prepared by the chef for the gala tonight.
A gourmet meal has been prepared by the chef for the gala tonight.
A gourmet meal is prepared by the chef for the gala tonight.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A gourmet meal is being prepared by the chef for the gala tonight.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The original sentence is in the **Present Continuous Tense**, indicated by the auxiliary verb **is** followed by the **present participle** form of the verb **preparing**.

• The standard rule for converting **Present Continuous Tense** from active to **Passive Voice** follows the structure: **New Subject + is/am/are + being + Past Participle (V3) + by + New Object**.

• The **Object** of the active sentence, **a gourmet meal**, transitions to the **Subject** position in the passive sentence.

• Because **a gourmet meal** is a **singular noun**, the auxiliary verb **is** is used, followed by the marker **being** to preserve the **continuous** nature of the action.

• The **Past Participle** of the verb **prepare** is **prepared**, which is used to satisfy the passive construction requirements.

• The **Subject** of the active sentence, **The chef**, becomes the **Agent** in the passive sentence and is introduced by the preposition **by**.

• The adverbial phrase **for the gala tonight** remains intact as it describes the **temporal and situational context** of the action.

 **Additional Information__**

• The distinction between different tenses in **Passive Voice** is crucial for selection:

• **Simple Present Passive**: Uses **is/am/are + V3** (e.g., is prepared). It is typically used for **facts or habits**.

• **Past Continuous Passive**: Uses **was/were + being + V3** (e.g., was being prepared). It describes an **interrupted or ongoing action** in the past.

• **Present Perfect Passive**: Uses **has/have + been + V3** (e.g., has been prepared). It indicates an **action completed** at an indefinite time in the past with current relevance.

</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?
Are the publishers organising a book signing event for the new author?

options.text: Was a book signing event being organised by the publishers for the new author?
Is a book signing event being organised by the new author for the publishers?
Is a book signing event being organised by the publishers for the new author?
Is a book signing event been organised for the new author by the publishers?

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Is a book signing event being organised by the publishers for the new author?**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The given sentence is an **interrogative sentence** in the **Present Continuous Tense**.

• The structure for an active voice sentence in the present continuous interrogative form is: **Is/Am/Are + Subject + Present Participle (V-ing) + Object?**.

• When converting this to **Passive Voice**, the structure changes to: **Is/Am/Are + New Subject (the original object) + being + Past Participle (V3) + by + New Object (the original subject)?**.

• The object of the active sentence is **a book signing event**. As this is a **singular noun**, the auxiliary verb **Is** remains appropriate for the start of the passive sentence.

• The verb **organising** must be converted into the passive continuous form, which is **being organised**.

• The original subject **the publishers** becomes the agent of the action, introduced by the preposition **by**.

• Following these grammatical rules, the construction becomes: **Is** (Auxiliary) + **a book signing event** (New Subject) + **being organised** (Passive Verb) + **by the publishers** (Agent) + **for the new author** (Recipient phrase).

 **Additional Information__**

• Distinctions between incorrect transformations:

• **Tense Consistency:** Passive voice must always maintain the **original tense**. Using **Was** shifts the sentence into the **Past Continuous**, which is grammatically incorrect for this context.

• **Being vs. Been:** The word **being** is used for **continuous tenses**, while **been** is used for **perfect tenses** (e.g., Has a book signing event **been** organised?).

• **Logical Meaning:** The passive voice should not alter the **logical relationship** between the actors; the publishers are the ones performing the action, not the author.

</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?
Let this mistake not be repeated.

options.text: No one will repeat this mistake.
This mistake let not be repeated

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Don't repeat this mistake.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The provided sentence 'Let this mistake not be repeated' is in the **Passive Voice** and follows the structure of a **Negative Imperative Sentence**.
 
• In **Passive Voice**, the construction for imperative sentences typically begins with **Let**, followed by the **Object**, then 'not' (for negative), the auxiliary **be**, and the **Past Participle (V3)** form of the verb.
 
• To convert this into the **Active Voice**, the sentence must start with the **Imperative Verb** or the negative marker **Do not (Don't)** because the subject 'You' is understood and omitted in such commands.
 
• The conversion follows the formula: **Do not / Don't + Verb (Base Form) + Object**.
 
• Identifying the components: The object is **'this mistake'** and the principal verb is **'repeat'**. Combining these according to the active voice rule results in **'Don't repeat this mistake'**.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Voice Transformation Rules**:
 
 
• **Imperative Sentences**: These express orders, requests, or advice. In the **Active Voice**, they usually begin with a verb. Example: 'Shut the door' (Active) becomes 'Let the door be shut' (Passive).
 
• **Prohibitions**: For sentences intended to stop an action, the **Active Voice** uses **Do not** or **Don't**. The corresponding **Passive Voice** uses the structure **Let + Object + not + be + V3**.
 
• **Tense Consistency**: Imperative sentences do not typically use modal auxiliaries like **will** or **won't** in their standard form, as those indicate the **Future Indefinite Tense** rather than an immediate command or prohibition.
 
• **Subject-Verb Relationship**: In the active form, the implied subject **You** is the agent performing the action of 'repeating'. In the passive form, the focus shifts to the **Object** (the mistake) receiving the action.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option which can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. In case Options A, B and C are not found suitable, choose Option D: "No Improvement Required."
The witness was unable to provide a statement consistent to the facts presented earlier in the court.

options.text: consistent with the facts presented earlier
consistent on the facts presented earlier
consistent of the facts present earlier

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**consistent with the facts presented earlier**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The sentence requires the correct **adjectival collocation** and **prepositional usage** for the word **consistent**.

• In English grammar, the adjective **consistent** is idiomatic and must be followed by the preposition **with** to indicate agreement, harmony, or compatibility between two or more elements.

• The phrase **consistent with** implies that the witness's **statement** does not contradict or vary from the **facts** already established in the **court**.

• The original phrase 'consistent to' is grammatically incorrect as **consistent** does not take the preposition **to** when used to show alignment between statements and evidence.

• The **past participle** **presented** is correctly used to modify **facts**, indicating that the presentation of evidence occurred at a prior time relative to the witness's statement.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Consistent with**:

• **Function**: It acts as an **adjective phrase** describing a state of being **congruent** or **in line with** a standard or previous occurrence.

• **Example**: The defendant's alibi was not **consistent with** the **forensic evidence** found at the scene.

• **Common Prepositional Errors**:

• **Consistent on**: Incorrect; the preposition **on** is generally used to denote **thematic focus** (e.g., 'consistent on the issue') rather than **structural alignment** between two statements.

• **Consistent of**: Often confused with the **phrasal verb** **consist of** (meaning 'to be composed of'). However, **consistent** is an adjective and does not utilize **of** to express compatibility.

• **Verb Tense and Form**:

• The use of the auxiliary verb **was** and the adverb **earlier** necessitates a **past participle** (**presented**) to function as a **reduced relative clause** (facts which were presented). Option 3 uses **present**, which fails to maintain the **past tense** narrative.

</ul

questions.question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. Until tea-time that day she had
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**__Key Points__**

 
• The paragraph describes the character of **Mr. Appin** and the surprising reveal of his discovery, moving from his mundane exterior to a world-altering claim.
 
• **Sentence B follows S1** as it directly elaborates on the lack of **cleverness** mentioned in the first sentence:
 
 
• 'He was neither a wit nor a croquet champion, a hypnotic force nor a begetter of amateur theatricals.'
 
 
 
• **Sentence D follows B** because it continues the negative description using a parallel structure ('Neither did...') and shifts the focus to his **exterior**:
 
 
• 'Neither did his exterior suggest the sort of man in whom women are willing to pardon a generous measure of mental deficiency.'
 
 
 
• **Sentence A is the third sentence** as it identifies the character as **Mr. Appin** and concludes the description of his ordinary and unimpressive persona:
 
 
• 'He had subsided into mere Mr. Appin, and the Cornelius seemed a piece of transparent baptismal bluff.'
 
 
 
• **Sentence C is the fourth sentence** because it introduces the sudden claim of a major **discovery**, creating a sharp contrast with the previous description:
 
 
• 'And now he was claiming to have launched on the world a discovery beside which the invention of gunpowder, of the printing-press, and of steam locomotion were inconsiderable trifles.'
 
 
 
• This discovery is the referent for 'this thing' in **S2**, which describes the discovery as more of a **miracle** than a scientific achievement.
 
• The correct sequence is **BDAC**.

 

**Coherent paragraph after rearrangement**:

'Until tea-time that day she had been unable to discover in what direction, if any, his cleverness lay. He was neither a wit nor a croquet champion, a hypnotic force nor a begetter of amateur theatricals. Neither did his exterior suggest the sort of man in whom women are willing to pardon a generous measure of mental deficiency. He had subsided into mere Mr. Appin, and the Cornelius seemed a piece of transparent baptismal bluff. And now he was claiming to have launched on the world a discovery beside which the invention of gunpowder, of the printing-press, and of steam locomotion were inconsiderable trifles. Science had made bewildering strides in many directions during recent decades, but this thing seemed to belong to the domain of miracle rather than to scientific achievement.'</div

questions.question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. Bateman Hunter slept badly.

A. But in a few hours now he would be in Chicago, and doubts assailed him.

B. For a fortnight on the boat that brought him from Tahiti to San Francisco he had been thinking of the story he had to tell, and for three days on the train he had repeated to himself the words in which he meant to tell it.

C. He was uncertain that he had done all that was possible, it was on his honour to do much more than the possible, and the thought was disturbing that, in a matter which so nearly touched his own interest, he had allowed his interest to prevail over his quixotry.

D. His conscience, always very sensitive, was not at ease.

S2. Self-sacrifice appealed so keenly to his imagination that the inability to exercise it gave him a sense of disillusion.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**__Key Points__**

 
• The paragraph describes the internal conflict and moral dilemma of **Bateman Hunter** during a journey. 
• **Sentence S1 is the first sentence** and establishes the initial state of the protagonist: 
• '**Bateman Hunter** slept badly.' 
• **Sentence B follows S1** as it provides the chronological context for his restlessness, detailing his long journey and the mental preparation of a story he intends to tell: 
• 'For a fortnight on the boat that brought him from **Tahiti** to **San Francisco** he had been thinking of the story he had to tell, and for **three days** on the train he had repeated to himself the words in which he meant to tell it.' 
• **Sentence A is the third sentence** because it shifts the focus to the imminent arrival in **Chicago** and the sudden onset of **doubts** that replace his prepared words: 
• 'But in a few hr now he would be in **Chicago**, and **doubts** assailed him.' 
• **Sentence D is the fourth sentence** as it explains the nature of those doubts by identifying the source as his sensitive **conscience**: 
• 'His **conscience**, always very sensitive, was not at ease.' 
• **Sentence C is the fifth sentence** because it elaborates on the specific moral struggle within his conscience, contrasting his **interest** with his **quixotry** (idealism): 
• 'He was uncertain that he had done all that was possible... and the thought was disturbing that... he had allowed his **interest** to prevail over his **quixotry**.' 
• **Sentence S2 is the final sentence**, concluding the thought by reflecting on how the protagonist's desire for **self-sacrifice** (quixotry) and his inability to act on it led to **disillusion**. 
• The correct sequence is **BADC**. 

 

**Coherent paragraph after rearrangement**:

'**Bateman Hunter** slept badly. For a fortnight on the boat that brought him from **Tahiti** to **San Francisco** he had been thinking of the story he had to tell, and for **three days** on the train he had repeated to himself the words in which he meant to tell it. But in a few hr now he would be in **Chicago**, and **doubts** assailed him. His **conscience**, always very sensitive, was not at ease. He was uncertain that he had done all that was possible, it was on his honour to do much more than the possible, and the thought was disturbing that, in a matter which so nearly touched his own interest, he had allowed his **interest** to prevail over his **quixotry**. **Self-sacrifice** appealed so keenly to his imagination that the inability to exercise it gave him a sense of **disillusion**.'</div

• The phrase **hardly any energy left** serves as a critical **contextual clue** in the sentence. In the context of **physical fatigue**, this usage is considered **pleonastic** or redundant.

• **Adjective Grading and Intensifiers**:
